setupSteps: Set the pad height. Most guides place the thigh pad so its top edge sits just below the hip bones (the front hip points), at the crease where the thigh meets the torso, so the hips are free to fold. If the pad rides up over the hip bones or the stomach, you will bend at the spine instead of the hip (coach-level; no source gave centimetres, Not found).

Set the ankle rollers. Hook the heels under the upper roller and press the front of the ankles against the lower roller (or sit the lower pad over the heel and Achilles area, depending on the machine). The rollers should hold you without crushing the ankle. Some benches adjust the roller distance so the hips sit correctly (product pages and guides, snippets only).
Feet and knees: feet shoulder-width or slightly wider, toes straight or turned out a little, knees soft but not bent.
Hands: cross the arms over the chest (easier), or place the fingertips behind the head (harder), or hold a plate against the chest (see section 7). Do not pull on the neck.
Start position: lock the body in a straight line from head to heels, head in line with the spine, eyes looking at the floor just ahead.

Pad height and rollers: same rule as above; the pad sits just below the hip bones and the ankles are locked under the rollers. At 90 degrees the body is parallel to the floor, so the hips must be clear of the pad's top edge to fold.

Starting position: body parallel to the floor, arms crossed on the chest. Hinge down by folding at the hips (not the spine) until you feel the hamstrings stretch, then rise to the straight line. Many guides say rise to level, not past level.
Check the angle setting: if your bench can be set to 45 or 90 degrees, a 90 degree set-up gives a shorter range and heavier top position, so use less load (coach-level).

steps.title: Step onto the bench and set your hips
steps.action: Place the hips on the pad, just below the hip bones, and slide the heels under the rollers.
steps.feel: Pad pressing the front of the upper thighs; ankles firmly held.
steps.visualCheck: Side: pad is below the hip bones; front: feet even and straight.

steps.title: Cross your arms
steps.action: Cross both arms over the chest, hands on the opposite shoulders.
steps.feel: Weight of the upper body hanging forward.

steps.title: Rise to the straight line
steps.action: Squeeze the buttocks and lift until the body forms a straight line from head to heels.
steps.feel: Buttocks and lower back switched on; no pinch.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders, hips and ankles in one straight line; chin level.

steps.title: Brace
steps.action: Gently tighten the stomach as if bracing for a light poke.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs not flared up; lower back not arched.

steps.title: Hinge forward
steps.action: Fold at the hips and lower the upper body slowly, back long and neutral, until the hamstrings feel a stretch.
steps.feel: Stretch behind the thighs; lower back stays steady.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back stays flat as the torso tips; neck stays in line with the spine; no rounding of the lower back.

steps.title: Pause at the bottom
steps.breathing: Hold the in-breath only for a moment, do not strain.
steps.visualCheck: Side: torso well below level, hips still on the pad.

steps.title: Rise by squeezing the glutes
steps.action: Drive the hips into the pad and lift the torso back up, leading with the buttocks, not by flinging the head up.
steps.feel: Glutes and hamstrings pushing, lower back supporting.
steps.visualCheck: Side: smooth lift, neck neutral, no head snapping back.

steps.title: Stop at the straight line
steps.action: Finish when the body is in a straight line and squeeze the buttocks for one second. Do not lean back or arch past the line.
steps.feel: Buttocks tight; lower back working but not pinched.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders, hips and ankles in a line; no deep curve in the lower back.

steps.title: Finish the set
steps.action: After the last rep, hinge slowly forward and step off the bench.
steps.visualCheck: Side: smooth, no jerk; walk away slowly.

commonMistakes.title: Arching past a straight line (hyperextension)
commonMistakes.text: Arching past a straight line (hyperextension). Why: loads the small joints and the discs at the end of the range, and the glutes stop doing the work. Fix: stop when the body is straight; squeeze the glutes; look at the floor.

commonMistakes.title: Pad set too high
commonMistakes.text: Pad set too high. Why: the hips cannot fold, so the lower spine does the bending. Fix: set the pad just below the hip bones.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging and bouncing at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Swinging and bouncing at the bottom. Why: momentum, shorter control and higher spinal stress. Fix: 2-3 s down, 1 s pause, 2 s up.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the lower back as you hinge down
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the lower back as you hinge down. Why: a flexed spine under load stresses the discs. Fix: keep the back long and hinge from the hips; use less range if you cannot keep it flat.

commonMistakes.title: Throwing the head back at the top
commonMistakes.text: Throwing the head back at the top. Why: strains the neck and shortens the hinge. Fix: neck stays in line with the spine.

commonMistakes.title: Using too much weight too soon
commonMistakes.text: Using too much weight too soon. Why: the plate pulls the torso forward and shifts the work to the spine. Fix: master 12-15 clean bodyweight reps before adding a plate.

commonMistakes.title: Hands pulling on the neck
commonMistakes.text: Hands pulling on the neck. Why: the neck bends forward and the hands help the lift. Fix: cross arms on the chest first; fingertips only if the neck stays neutral.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure briefly. Fix: breathe in as you lower and out as you rise.

commonMistakes.title: Ankle rollers too loose
commonMistakes.text: Ankle rollers too loose. Why: the legs shift and the hinge slips. Fix: adjust the rollers before the first rep.

safetyNotes: Lower back: the lower back muscles work hard at the top; the exercise is not for acute back pain or a flare-up.
Disc and spine: ACE-related guidance lists disc disease, sciatica and stenosis among conditions needing particular care; some people feel better with extension, others do not.

Osteoporosis: the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation advises avoiding trunk flexion exercise and says trunk extension and abdominal stabilisation exercise are safe for people at high fracture risk; Mayo Clinic advises avoiding bending forward at the waist. A loaded hinge forward is a flexion move, so ask a professional.
Spotter: not needed for bodyweight or light plate. Ask staff to check the pad height the first time.
Gym etiquette: wipe the pad and rollers, return the plate, do not film other members.
